trace.goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.
expected_facts: Early-stage startups can sell to CIOs if the value is differentiated and the risk to the buyer is contained.
CIO trust matters more than polish on day one; founders need credibility, responsiveness, and a plan to close gaps.
Founders should not try to bypass enterprise constraints entirely; they should frame the relationship as a pragmatic pilot with clear ROI.
rubric_must_haves: Explains why trust and buyer risk matter in enterprise sales.
Includes at least one concrete example, scenario, or metric.
Sounds like direct operator advice rather than generic enterprise-sales theory.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer argues that even a tiny SaaS team can sell to a CIO, but only when the founder understands the buyer's social contract: do not create career risk, be honest about what is missing, show fast ROI, and build trust directly. The piece should emphasize that CIOs can back startups when the upside is meaningful and the initial blast radius is small.

trace.answer: So we're all here talking about how startups sell to big companies and I think one thing you'll see consistently when you go out there on the road is, most people don't have the guts for it. And so this week in my series on SaaStr, I want to talk about something I call the social contract. Because every time I've gone out there and sold to large corporations, what I found was if they wanted you, then no matter where you were -- whether you had two customers, three customers, five customers, 50 customers -- they would figure out a way to get you into their environment. Now, why do I bring up these two gentlemen? Well, because they're CIOs. They came to our little tiny event called DEMO in 2012. It wasn't very big, just a few hundred folks. But we had some amazing speakers and they came. And let me tell you, if someone wants your product bad enough, even though you're a small company with limited resources, they will find a way to work around those issues. Now, I'm sure this is nothing new to many of us in sales. What's important, though, is understanding the social contract. So the social contract is basically saying that once you've gained the trust of the buyer, which in larger organizations often means the VP of Engineering, the head of IT, whoever it is -- whatever it is -- once they believe in you and your product, they will bend over backwards to help you succeed. They will move mountains to make sure you win.
